newsitem.title: Indonesia: Indonesia mining sector on edge over changes.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia mining sector on edge over changes.

text.p: A cloud of uncertainty hung over Indonesia's mining sector on Friday as the government sought to amend coal mining rules days after proposing sweeping changes to regulations governing the exploitation of minerals.
As foreign companies scrambled to submit their response to the proposals before the Tuesday deadline, a senior minister indicated the proposed changes might be watered down.
The minister, who declined to be identified, said the government was concerned the changes proposed by the Mines and Energy Ministry might impair the overall investment climate.
"We are concerned the investment climate will be affected by the proposals," the minister told Reuters. "We might have to take another look at them."
State Secretary Murdiono told reporters on Thursday the government would be consistent with its policy that allowed 100 percent foreign-owned companies to operate in the country.
Investment Minister Sanyoto Sastrowardoyo said he was not aware of the reasons or motivation behind the proposals.
Under the proposed changes for the minerals mining sector, foreign companies are required to allocate at least a 10 percent stake in future ventures to the government for free.

The companies would also be required to share capital gains made in stock exchanges outside Indonesia with their shareholders, and the raising of additional capital through a public offering of shares must be done in Indonesia.
The government informed mining companies on Thursday that similar changes would be made to the coal sector.
A copy of the proposed changes obtained by Reuters showed that coal companies had to divest 51 percent of their equity in projects to Indonesians by the 10th year of operations.
"During our discussions with the government, we were given the impression that the divestment policy would not be included in the coal contract of work," one senior foreign miner said.
"Also, the formula for determining the price is vague and seems to be weighted in favour of the buyer," he added.

He said the divestment price formula was clearly spelled out in the existing contract, while that for the third generation contract merely stated "...terms and conditions reasonably intended and in good faith to Indonesian participants".
"The message we are getting unofficially is that senior officials in the (mines and energy) ministry are not supporting this," another foreign mining executive said.
"The proposal on the 10-percent equity to be given to the government seems to run counter to an existing regulation that allows 100-percent foreign-owned companies to operate in Indonesia," he said.
"Now they are suggesting a foreign company cannot operate 100 percent," he said, adding that next Tuesday's deadline left companies with little time to respond effectively to the move.

Meanwhile, the secretary-general of the Indonesian Mining Association, Benny Wahyu, said the group had written to Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana seeking a meeting to discuss the proposals.
Sudjana has yet to return from Vienna, where he attended the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) meeting that ended on Thursday.
